title: How to add a video to a slide in Keynote on Mac: step by step
metaTitle: How to Add a Video to a Slide in Keynote on Mac | Lazur
description: Learn how to add a video to a slide in Keynote on Mac: insert from Photos, drag from Finder, or embed a YouTube or Vimeo link.

intro: Click Insert Media in the Keynote toolbar, choose Choose Photos or Videos, select your file, then drag it onto the slide. You can also drag a video straight from Finder, or paste a YouTube or Vimeo link under Add Web Video.
tldr: Click Insert Media in the toolbar, choose Choose Photos or Videos, then pick your file.
Or drag a video from Finder onto a media placeholder or anywhere on the slide.
For YouTube or Vimeo, use Insert Media > Add Web Video and paste the link. Playback needs internet.
If the file won't import, convert it to a QuickTime .mov with QuickTime Player, iMovie or Compressor.

blocks.text: Two things decide whether the video works: the file and your version of Keynote. Apple says a video must be in a format QuickTime can play on your Mac, and it suggests a QuickTime .mov file. Apple's support pages also list Keynote 15.4 for Mac, which requires macOS 26 or later. Check both before you start, so you don't lose ten minutes to a file that won't import.
Check the video file and your Mac first

Start with a quick test. Open the video in QuickTime Player. If it plays there, Keynote is more likely to accept it. If QuickTime can't open it, Keynote is unlikely to play it either, and you should convert the file first. Apple's own check is to select the file in Finder and press Command-I to read its Kind. That shows the real format, which helps when a file extension looks wrong.

items: Format: a file QuickTime can open. Apple suggests .mov.
Keynote version: Keynote 15.4 for Mac, according to Apple's Creator Studio page.
macOS: macOS 26 or later for Keynote for Mac, according to the same page.
File size: a presentation over 500 MB may run better when saved as a package file.
Internet: needed only if the video is a YouTube or Vimeo link.

blocks.title: Two macOS requirements
blocks.text: Apple's Creator Studio page says Keynote for Mac needs macOS 26 or later. Apple's newsroom says the Creator Studio version of Keynote needs macOS Sequoia 15.6 or later. Check your Mac's version before you update.
Add a video from your Mac with Insert Media

This is the method Apple documents first. Select the slide, click the Insert Media button in the toolbar, then click Choose Photos or Videos. Pick the file and drop it onto the slide. The steps below follow that order, with the keyboard shortcut at the end for people who prefer to skip the menus.

Plan the slide before you add the clip. Leave room around the video for a title or a caption. A video that fills the whole slide can hide labels you still need. You don't have to use full screen. You can shrink the clip and place it beside your text.
Drag a video in from Finder

Dragging is often faster than the menus. Open the folder with your video in Finder, then move the Finder window so you can see the slide in Keynote at the same time. Drag the video file onto a media placeholder, or anywhere else on the slide. Apple's guide says both drop targets work.

If the Finder window covers the slide, shrink it first. Dragging works best when both windows are fully visible. Drop the file too early and it lands on the wrong slide, so check the thumbnail on the left before you let go.
Use a media placeholder for the video

A media placeholder is a spot on the slide that waits for media. Apple's keyboard shortcut list calls the command Define the object as a media placeholder, and the shortcut is ⌃⌥⌘I. Select the shape you want to use, press that shortcut, then drag your video onto it. Use this when a slide design already has an area for pictures or video. If you don't see a placeholder, drop the video anywhere on the slide instead.
Add a YouTube or Vimeo video with a link

A web video stays on the internet. The slide holds a link, not the video file, so the presentation stays small. The trade-off is simple. The video needs a connection when you present, so test on the network you will use on the day.

items: Click the Insert Media button in the toolbar.
Type or paste the YouTube or Vimeo link.

blocks.text: Apple says web video needs an internet connection to play. Check that it plays in the slideshow, not just in the editor. If the venue Wi-Fi is weak, keep a local copy of the same clip ready as a backup.

blocks.text: Set when the video plays

Apple's guide is not consistent here. One sentence says a video plays when its slide appears. Another says that by default the video and audio plays when you click it during a presentation. Don't trust either one blindly. Build a test slide, run the slideshow, and watch what happens on your version.

blocks.title: Test before you present
blocks.text: Run the slideshow from the Play button, then click the video. If it waits for a click and you wanted it to start on its own, check the Movie tab in the Format sidebar. Apple's pages don't list every playback control, so look at your own sidebar.
Replace a video you already added

Replacing keeps the slide and swaps in a new clip. Select the video on the slide. Open the Format sidebar. Click the Movie tab, then click Replace, and pick the new file. The Format sidebar also has Movie, Audio and Web Video tabs, so check which tab is open if you don't see Replace.
Fix a video that won't import or play

Start with the file, not with Keynote. Apple suggests checking whether the file is damaged or in an unsupported format. Then check for macOS updates, and try an app that supports the format, such as QuickTime Player. If the file plays in QuickTime but not in Keynote, the format or a Keynote setting is the likely cause.

blocks.text: Keynote can also convert some formats as you add them. Open Keynote > Settings > General. Under Adding Media, you'll see two checkboxes: Optimize media for iPhone, iPad, and Apple Vision Pro, and Optimize media for older devices. With both on, HEVC, HEIC and ProRes convert to H.264, JPEG or PNG. The settings apply only to media you add after the change.
Shrink a presentation that got too big

Video makes presentations big fast. Apple's Reduce File Size tool sits in the File menu. Go to File > Reduce File Size, choose a movie option, then set Movie Quality, which sets the maximum resolution of your video. Work on a copy while you learn how the tool behaves.

items: Most compatible (H.264): the first movie option Apple lists.
High efficiency (HEVC): the second movie option Apple lists.
Preserve original format: keeps the video in its current format.

blocks.text: Read the warnings. Apple says a mix of options can make the file larger, so check the size after you save. Reduce This File changes the original. Reduce a Copy leaves the original unchanged. For a first attempt, use Reduce a Copy.

If the presentation is over 500 MB, or holds large video or image files, Apple says Keynote may run better as a package file. Some web and email services don't accept package files. Export a copy in a format the other person can open before you send it.
Limits with Keynote for iCloud

Keynote for iCloud handles video differently from the Mac app. Apple says it cannot add a new live video object there. Existing live video objects can be edited, but they don't access your camera when you present. On iCloud.com, movies and audio don't play during slide transitions. The soundtrack and recorded voiceover don't play either.

Playback works in Keynote for Mac, iPhone and iPad. Apple's iCloud page doesn't say whether YouTube or Vimeo web videos play in Keynote for iCloud. Don't assume they do. If your slide uses a web video, build and test it in Keynote for Mac.
Add subtitles to a video

Subtitles need macOS 26.4 or later, according to Apple's guide. Start the slideshow from the Play button, click the video, then click Closed Captions. Check that option on your version before you promise captions to an audience.
Mistakes people make with video in Keynote

items: Testing only in edit view. Apple says videos play on click during a presentation, so run the slideshow.
Dropping in a file QuickTime can't open, then blaming Keynote.
Turning on the optimize settings and expecting old videos to change.
Using Reduce This File and losing the original clip.
Relying on a web video at a venue with unreliable internet.

blocks.text: Each of these costs time on the day you present. Find them a day early, and the slide behaves the same on stage.
What to do next

Once the video plays, you may want to share the slides as a film. Read [How to export a presentation as a movie in Keynote on Mac](/how-to/export-a-presentation-as-a-movie-in-keynote). If you present from notes, [How to add presenter notes in Keynote on Mac](/how-to/add-presenter-notes-in-keynote) covers the next step.

faq.question: Can I add a YouTube video to a Keynote slide on Mac?
faq.answer: Yes. Click Insert Media, choose Add Web Video, paste the YouTube or Vimeo link, then click Insert. Apple says an internet connection is needed to play web video, so test it on the network you will use.

faq.question: Do I need to convert my video before adding it to Keynote?
faq.answer: Only if QuickTime can't open it. Apple says the video must be in a format QuickTime supports, and it suggests a QuickTime .mov file. Convert with QuickTime Player, iMovie or Compressor when the file won't import.

faq.question: Does the video play automatically when the slide appears?
faq.answer: Apple's guide gives two answers. One sentence says it plays when the slide appears. Another says that by default it plays when you click it during a presentation. Run the slideshow in your version to see which one applies.

faq.question: Can I add video in Keynote for iCloud?
faq.answer: Apple says Keynote for iCloud cannot add a new live video object. Movies also don't play during slide transitions there. Playback works in Keynote for Mac, iPhone and iPad, so use Keynote for Mac for a presentation with video.

faq.question: Will reducing the file size change my video?
faq.answer: It can. Reduce This File changes the original, while Reduce a Copy leaves it unchanged. Apple also warns that some option combinations can make the file larger, so check the result before you share it.

faq.question: Which macOS do I need for Keynote 15.4?
faq.answer: Apple's Creator Studio page says Keynote for Mac requires macOS 26 or later. Apple's newsroom says the Creator Studio version needs macOS Sequoia 15.6 or later. Check the requirement on Apple's page for your region before you update.

steps.name: Open the slide
steps.text: Open your presentation in Keynote. In the slide navigator on the left, click the slide where the video belongs. The slide appears in the main canvas.

steps.name: Click Insert Media
steps.text: In the toolbar at the top of the window, click the Insert Media button. Apple's guide uses this label. Some newer pages may say Media instead.
steps.tip: Apple's pages use both labels in places. If the wording differs, look for the media button in the toolbar.

steps.name: Choose Photos or Videos
steps.text: Click Choose Photos or Videos from the options. A file window opens so you can find the video on your Mac.

steps.name: Pick the video file
steps.text: Find the video and select it. Confirm your choice in the file window. Keynote adds the video to the slide.

steps.name: Drop the video onto the slide
steps.text: Drag the video onto a media placeholder, or anywhere on the slide. Let go when it sits where you want it.

steps.name: Resize and move the video
steps.text: Click the video to select it. Drag a corner handle to resize it. Drag the video itself to move it.

steps.name: Test the playback
steps.text: Click the Play button in the toolbar to start the slideshow from this slide. Click the video to play it. Apple says videos play on click by default.
steps.tip: Run the whole slideshow once. Apple's pages disagree on timing, so the test is the only proof.

steps.name: Use the keyboard shortcut
steps.text: To skip the menus, press ⇧⌘V. Apple lists this shortcut as Choose a file to insert. Pick the file as you did in the earlier step.
steps.tip: Some shortcuts can be changed in System Settings, so the key may differ on your Mac.

shortcuts.action: Define the object as a media placeholder

troubleshooting.fix: Check that QuickTime Player opens the file. If it won't, convert it to a QuickTime .mov with QuickTime Player, iMovie or Compressor, then insert the new file.

troubleshooting.problem: The video inserts but won't play
troubleshooting.fix: Select the file in Finder and press ⌘I to check its Kind. Check for macOS updates, then try an app that supports the format, as Apple suggests.

troubleshooting.problem: Old videos still fail after you change settings
troubleshooting.fix: The Optimize media settings in Keynote > Settings > General apply only to media added afterward. Remove the video and add it again.

troubleshooting.problem: Video doesn't play when you expect
troubleshooting.fix: Apple's pages give conflicting timing, so test in the slideshow. Check the Movie tab in the Format sidebar for playback options.

troubleshooting.problem: The file is too large to send
troubleshooting.fix: Use File > Reduce File Size on a copy. If the presentation is over 500 MB, save it as a package file, but don't send package files through services that reject them.
